text: PAM — Pluggable Authentication Modules — is the framework login, sudo, su, and sshd all call into instead of each checking a password themselves. This lesson covers what PAM actually does, how its config under /etc/pam.d/ is organized, and two of its real modules: pam_unix.so for the password check itself, and pam_faillock.so for locking an account out after too many failed attempts.

Every one of those programs hands authentication off to libpam, which reads a config file matching that service's name — /etc/pam.d/sudo, /etc/pam.d/sshd, /etc/pam.d/login — and runs a stack of modules to decide allow or deny. That's the entire point: add a new policy, like account lockout, to the shared stack once, and login, sudo, and ssh all get it without a single line of their own source code changing.

Most PAM stacks share a common file like system-auth rather than repeating themselves, and near the bottom of that stack sits auth required pam_unix.so — the module that checks a typed password against the hashed value stored in /etc/shadow. It's the traditional Unix password check, present in nearly every PAM configuration as the baseline authentication step, and if it's removed from the stack, that password check disappears along with it.

pam_faillock.so stacks on top of that baseline: deny=5 locks an account after five failed attempts, and unlock_time=900 releases the lock automatically after fifteen minutes. preauth checks for an existing lockout before the password is even checked; authfail records a failure once pam_unix denies. The bracketed control-flag syntax, like [success=1 default=bad], decides what happens next in the stack based on each module's result — that's what makes stacking multiple modules together possible at all. It's a real, working defense against brute-force password guessing against login, sudo, or ssh — all three, from one config change.

That's PAM in outline: one framework, a stack of pluggable modules per service, read out of /etc/pam.d/. Next up: Linux file permissions past basic rwx — real access control lists with setfacl and getfacl, and the sticky bit that protects shared directories like /tmp.
